transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-08-21
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Ortega (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE); Alex Rivera (CTO, Solara), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Tom Gallagher (Infra), Ellen Park (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on Solara's need for dedicated GPU capacity: isolation for IP and PII, predictable throughput for inference on production models, and ability to burst for seasonal demand. Discussed autoscaling patterns, isolation options (VPC/on-prem), fallback to hosted, and security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO). Agreed to run a pilot benchmark with committed reserved nodes and burst pool; Redwood to share pricing and security docs.

Transcript:
00:00 Jamie Ortega: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jamie from Redwood, i'm the AE on this. We brought Maya and Liam from the engineering side. quick intro?
00:08 Alex Rivera: Hey Alex here, CTO at Solara. we run forecasting models and a few customer-facing chat assistants used by our field techs. priority is isolation and cost predictability.
00:16 Priya Singh: Priya, ML eng. i'm focused on latency SLOs and model quality; we have both streaming and batch use cases.
00:22 Tom Gallagher: Tom infra lead. i handle VPCs and network peering and security.
00:28 Jamie Ortega: Great. quick agenda: understand current stack, volumes and peaks, constraints, and what dedicated would look like. Maya, do you want to kick into questions on traffic and model details?
00:36 Maya Chen: sure yeah. Priya, can you describe the models you'll serve? size, quantization, typical sequence lengths?
00:42 Priya Singh: mostly 34B-ish offline models converted to a trimmed runtime, we run a fine-tuned 13B for chat and a few 70B-ish encoder-decoder for summarization. typical seq len for chat is 512 tokens, summaries go up to 2k tokens; per-request we see median latency needs of <300ms for chat. throughput is variable, baseline about 30 req/s but during some campaigns spikes to ~250 req/s over a 10-15 minute window.
01:10 Maya Chen: ok that's helpful. are those running on your infra today or cloud endpoints?
01:14 Priya Singh: currently on AWS EC2 G5/G5n on prem-ish; we also do experiments on hosted LLM endpoints but costs got wild for bursty traffic. that's why we're exploring Redwood Dedicated for reserved GPUs + a burst strategy.
01:26 Jamie Ortega: makes sense. Alex, what are the must-haves for dedicated?
01:30 Alex Rivera: isolation (we can't mix other customers on same hardware), encryption at rest + KMS, audit logs for every inference for compliance, and predictable monthly spend. also ability to scale up for campaigns — e.g., marketing push that drives 5x traffic for an hour.
01:46 Maya Chen: Redwood Dedicated offers reserved pools with isolation — you can get tenant-isolated GPU pools (single-tenant hosts) or VPC-backed private deployments. For bursts we do two patterns: reserved baseline plus a burst pool that uses shared capacity with a cost premium, or bursting within your reserved pool by pre-warming extra nodes. we can also set automated fallback to hosted variants for non-sensitive traffic.
02:10 Tom Gallagher: how does the VPC peering work? we need IP allowlists and flow logs in our SIEM.
02:16 Maya Chen: we support VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink for certain regions; we can provide static egress IPs for allowlisting and we stream flow logs and audit logs to your S3 or log destination. KMS integration is customer-managed.
02:30 Priya Singh: about latency — you mentioned pre-warming; do you have numbers for cold-starts and tail latency when scaling up?
02:36 Maya Chen: cold-starts depend on model size and quantization. for a 13B quantized model typical scale-up time is under 60 seconds with fast prefetch pipelines; 34B/70B can be a couple minutes. we use continuous batching and KV cache warmup to reduce token latency after scale-up. tail latency during aggressive scale-ups can spike — we recommend canary capacity or a small buffer in reserved capacity to avoid user-visible tail spikes.
03:06 Jamie Ortega: to add — many customers maintain a 10-20% buffer of reserved capacity specifically for headroom; Redwood's autoscaler can trigger warm-ups earlier based on traffic forecasts.
03:16 Alex Rivera: ok cost question — what's unit economics look like for reserved vs burst?
03:20 Maya Chen: reserved is a commit-based discount (monthly/annual), lower per-token cost. burst pool charged at higher rate and subject to capacity; alternative is dedicated burst nodes which are billed at a mid-tier. we will send a pricing matrix. in practice customers balance by putting latency-sensitive and sensitive-data traffic on reserved and non-sensitive bulk inference on burst/hosted.
03:44 Priya Singh: do you support multi-tenant within our account? we want app-level isolation — different teams in our company shouldn't see each other's models.
03:52 Liam Patel: yes, we support per-route RBAC, per-model namespaces, and token-level access controls; plus audit trails for every request.
04:00 Tom Gallagher: any limitations for on-prem deployment? data residency is important; we may need an air-gapped option for some contracts.
04:07 Maya Chen: we have a Private deployment that ships a customer-managed control plane and runtime; it supports air-gapped installs with HSM/KMS integrations. there are extra ops requirements and a heavier pricing model but it's doable.
04:20 Alex Rivera: about model updates and rollouts — how do you handle versioning and canarying? we can't have a bad rollout affect all field agents.
04:28 Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports model pinning, canary deploys and traffic splitting. you can route X% of traffic to new model, and automatic rollback if quality/regression metrics cross thresholds. we can also do per-route fallback to a previous model for degraded quality.
04:42 Priya Singh: test harness — can we run synthetic traffic in a pilot? measure p95/p99 and cost per token?
04:48 Jamie Ortega: absolutely that's the plan for the pilot we'll run benchmarks with your prompt set and token distributions, capture p50/p95/p99, and produce a cost estimate under reserved vs burst scenarios.
04:56 Tom Gallagher: network egress and private data — if we use hosted burst, does data leave our VPC?
05:02 Maya Chen: if bursting uses Redwood shared pool, traffic will egress to Redwood's environment but we support contracts that limit logging retention and ensure PII redaction. for fully private requirements you should pick Dedicated with private VPC or Private on-prem.
05:16 Alex Rivera: what's the SLA for Dedicated?
05:20 Jamie Ortega: for Dedicated we have an SLA that targets 99.9% uptime and latency targets per model class; exact SLA depends on committed tier and region. we can include an enterprise SLA in the contract.
05:30 Priya Singh: any features for caching/prefix caching to reduce repeated cost?
05:34 Maya Chen: yes we have KV prefix cache that can be colocated with the serving runtime. if you're doing similar prompts we can cache tokens to avoid re-computation, highly effective for multi-turn dialogs.
05:46 Alex Rivera: security — SSO, SCIM, RBAC — all supported?
05:50 Liam Patel: SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, per-route RBAC, and detailed audit logs. we can also integrate with your KMS for envelope keys.
05:58 Priya Singh: do you support quantization workflows? we quantize to 4-bit/8-bit?
06:02 Maya Chen: we support quantization-friendly runtimes and recommend certain profiles based on model architecture; 4-bit quantization works for many models with minor quality tradeoffs — we'll share recommended quant profiles for your model zoo.
06:14 Tom Gallagher: what about backups and snapshots for model weights and who handles those?
06:18 Maya Chen: in Dedicated, Redwood manages model lifecycle; we store model artifacts in encrypted storage, snapshots are versioned, and we can provide offline snapshots to your storage if needed. for Private, customer-managed.
06:28 Alex Rivera: can we do a hybrid — some models on your dedicated and the most sensitive on-prem?
06:32 Jamie Ortega: yes, hybrid is common. you can route sensitive workloads to Private and keep more general workloads on Dedicated. the Console supports routing rules.
06:40 Priya Singh: operationally, how fast can we provision reserved nodes? what's lead time?
06:44 Maya Chen: provisioning a reserved pool typically takes 48-72 hours for standard setups; for special hardware or air-gapped deployments it's longer (weeks). we can provision a small trial pool faster for pilot.
06:56 Tom Gallagher: fine. for the pilot, we need pre-approved IP ranges and a runbook for failover.
07:02 Jamie Ortega: we'll include a runbook and network checklist. Maya we'll need a sample autoscale policy and a recommended reserved/burst split for their traffic pattern.
07:12 Maya Chen: noted. based on the 30 -> 250 rps spikes, i'd recommend baseline reserved capacity for ~50% of peak and a burst pool for the rest, plus 10-15% headroom. we'll draft specifics with expected p95 numbers.
07:26 Alex Rivera: what's the cancellation or contract flexibility? we want termination terms if usage is under-committed.
07:32 Jamie Ortega: contracts usually have a 12-month commit with step-downs; we can negotiate a pilot-to-production transition and flexible terms for the first 3 months.
07:40 Priya Singh: any known issues with certain model types? transformer encoder-decoder vs decoder-only performance differences?
07:46 Maya Chen: encoder-decoder workloads (seq2seq) have different memory patterns; we choose kernels accordingly. some older kernels favor decoder-only for lower latency but our runtime handles both and we can tune per-model.
07:58 Tom Gallagher: ok next steps summarised?
08:02 Jamie Ortega: i'll read them: 1) Send pricing and performance spreadsheet. 2) Share SOC2 and network diagram. 3) Maya to propose autoscale and burst config. 4) Schedule pilot for week of Aug 25 with synthetic workload. 5) Tom to share infra diagram and IP ranges.
08:18 Alex Rivera: that sounds right. thank you.

Close:
08:22 Jamie Ortega: great, we'll follow up via email with the docs and calendar invite for the pilot. thanks everyone.
08:28 Priya Singh: thanks all.

Notes on transcription: minor mis-hears on model sizes (34B sometimes transcribed as 'thirty-fourteen B' in earlier auto exports), some speaker attribution corrected manually.

End of transcript.
